data.outcome_summary: This OECD report uses PIAAC log-file data to study how adults allocate time to items and how disengagement relates to performance in low-stakes, untimed computer-based testing. The excerpted chapters focus on timing indicators (time on task, time to first interaction, time since last action) and on disengagement indicators (rapid item skipping and T-disengagement) derived from item-level response processes. The analysis is restricted to computer-based literacy and numeracy modules, excluding PSTRE in the timing/disengagement sections shown, and it leverages the adaptive/rotated design to interpret module-order effects and item-position patterns. At the item level, time on task is strongly correlated with time to first interaction and increases with item difficulty; respondents spend less time on items in the second module, accompanied by lower correctness and higher missingness. At the respondent level, time allocation follows a rational pattern relative to ex ante probability of success, and time on task shows a positive but declining association with the probability of giving a correct answer, with higher returns in Module 2. The report emphasizes that log-based time is an imperfect proxy for effort and that causal interpretation is limited because time and performance are jointly determined and log files do not reveal the cognitive strategies used.
